There isn't one best combo, because it depends on whether you'll run the roof A/C. The sources I read were thin on specific solar panel models. They were stronger on power stations, so my panel advice is mostly about sizing.

## Picks by RV use

**Full-time boondocking or running A/C: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**
- It has 4,096Wh (expandable past 12kWh), 4,000W continuous and 8,000W surge. That's enough to start a 13,500 BTU roof A/C.
- It recharges from 0 to 80% in about 50 minutes on AC.
- It's heavy, and the sources call moving it a two-person job.
- [Check it on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=ecoflow+delta+pro+3&tag=ggref-20). The source doesn't list a price. (Source: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))

**Weekend A/C and simple controls: Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro**
- It has 3,024Wh, 3,000W continuous and 6,000W surge, with physical buttons and an optional app.
- It has no 30A RV outlet, so you need a dogbone adapter.
- It weighs about 64 lb.
- [Check it on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=jackery+explorer+3000+pro&tag=ggref-20). (Source: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))

**Value with a built-in 30A RV port: BLUETTI AC200L**
- It has 2,048Wh and 2,400W continuous, and it takes solar directly.
- Fan noise is noticeable at full load, and there's no 240V output.
- 2,048Wh drains fast with an A/C running.
- [Check it on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=bluetti+ac200l&tag=ggref-20). (Source: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))

**Big capacity for the money: ALLPOWERS R4000**
- It has 3,456Wh of LiFePO4, 3,600W at 120V, an RV outlet and 2,000W of solar input. It also has a 5-year warranty.
- It weighs 45 kg (about 99 lb), so it stays put in the RV.
- Dealectric lists it at $1,499, or $1,319.12 with code EXTRA12. The code expires 2026-11-15 and was cart-tested on 10/23. Prices change, so check at checkout.
- [Buy at ALLPOWERS](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh). This is an affiliate link. Dealectric earns a commission, and the page says that pays for its code testing. (Source: [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/lab/V8/allpowers-r4000-3456wh))

**Small trailer or solo trips: Goal Zero Yeti 1500X**
- It has 1,516Wh and weighs about 44 lb.
- It needs a soft-start kit to run an A/C.
- [Check it on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=goal+zero+yeti+1500x&tag=ggref-20). (Source: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))

## Solar panels
- **Sizing:** A 300–400W folding array can refill a mid-size station in about one good summer day. Expect less in spring and fall.
- **Input limits:** Check each station's solar input before buying panels. The R4000 takes up to 2,000W across three inputs, with 650W max per input. [Acquired Sense](https://www.acquiredsense.com/reviews/power-stations.html) says the EcoFlow and Bluetti flagships accept the most solar, and it likes Jackery's SolarSaga panels.
- **A/C is hard to run on solar:** A roof A/C draws about 1,500W, so it will drain a battery in roughly 2 hours however much solar you add. Solar mostly covers the fridge, lights, laptop and Starlink.

## Caveats
- The best-known comparison I read ([Outdoor Power Stations](https://outdoorpowerstations.com/articles/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti)) covers older models, such as the AC200P. Its 700W solar cap and 2-year warranty don't apply to newer units like the AC200L.
- EmergencyEnergy is an Ontario site. Its specs apply in the US, but ignore its Canadian electrical-code notes. In the US, have an electrician do any hardwired transfer-switch work.
- Most of these pages carry affiliate links, including the Amazon links above.

## Where I'd start
Tell me your RV's amperage (30 or 50A), whether you need to run the A/C off-grid, and your budget. I can then narrow this to one station and a panel size.

For A/C off-grid, I'd go with the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, or the R4000 if price matters more. If you only need the fridge, lights and electronics, the AC200L plus 300–400W of folding panels is the cheaper route.

 Jackery vs EcoFlow vs Bluetti: Ultimate Brand Comparison 2026
 Updated: August 2026 • 10 min read
 If you're shopping for a portable power station in 2026, three names keep coming up: Jackery, EcoFlow, and Bluetti. They're the big three — together they control roughly 70% of the portable power station market. But they take very different approaches to design, pricing, and features. This is the comparison I wish I'd read before buying my first power station. Let's break it down.
 📊 June 2026 Market Update: Prices have stabilized after supply chain improvements. Jackery holds steady at $1,899 for the 2000 Plus. EcoFlow launched the Delta 3 series in Q1 2026 but the Delta Pro remains better value for home backup. Bluetti's AC200P at $1,299 is the most affordable 2,000Wh station from a major brand — though the 700W solar input limit hasn't improved. Anker (not in this three-way comparison but worth watching) now competes aggressively at the $1,599 price point with the SOLIX F2000.
[Check current prices on Amazon →](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=portable+power+station&tag=08191509-20)
 Brand Overviews
 Jackery — The Pioneer
 Founded in 2012 in California, Jackery basically created the portable power station category as we know it. They're the most recognized brand and the one your neighbor has probably heard of. Their design philosophy is Apple-like: polished, user-friendly, and premium-priced. Jackery stations rarely have the best specs on paper, but they consistently deliver the smoothest out-of-box experience. Their Explorer series is iconic and their expansion system is the most elegant on the market.
 EcoFlow — The Innovator
 Founded in 2017 by former DJI engineers, EcoFlow came in hot with the Delta series and its game-changing X-Boost and multi-charge technology. They aim for the highest specs: fastest charging, highest output, most features. EcoFlow's ecosystem extends beyond power stations into smart home panels, portable air conditioners (the Wave 2), and even a battery-powered fridge. If you want cutting-edge tech and maximum expandability, EcoFlow is the brand.
 Bluetti — The Value King
 Bluetti (formerly MaxOak) launched the AC200 in 2020 and disrupted the market with aggressive pricing. Their philosophy is simple: give you the most watt-hours and the most outlets for the least money. Bluetti stations sometimes lag on software polish, solar input speed, and app features — but they're almost always the best deal in terms of raw capacity per dollar.

 Build Quality and Design
 Jackery wins on fit and finish. The Explorer 2000 Plus feels like a premium consumer electronics product — smooth edges, tight seams, satisfying button clicks. The orange-accented design is instantly recognizable. Everything about the physical experience feels intentional.
 EcoFlow goes for rugged utility. The Delta Pro is built like a tank — thick plastic, reinforced corners, heavy-duty wheels. It's designed to be moved in and out of job sites, RVs, and garages. It's not pretty, but it's durable.
 Bluetti is utilitarian. The AC200P has a boxy, functional design with slightly cheaper-feeling plastics. The handle is basic. But nothing feels fragile or poorly assembled — it's just not as polished as the other two.
 Winner: Jackery for looks, EcoFlow for durability.
 App and Software Experience
 EcoFlow has the best app by a wide margin. Real-time energy monitoring, customizable charge/discharge schedules, X-Boost toggling, firmware OTA updates, and Alexa/Google Home integration. You can see per-port power draw and set battery reserve levels for outages. It's genuinely useful.
 Jackery comes second with a clean, reliable app. WiFi + Bluetooth, remote monitoring, port toggling, and firmware updates. It's simpler than EcoFlow's but more reliable — I've never had a connection drop with the Jackery app.
 Bluetti is a distant third. Bluetooth only, no WiFi, no remote monitoring, no scheduling, no OTA firmware updates. You have to load firmware via SD card. The app shows basic info (battery %, input/output watts) but that's about it.
 Winner: EcoFlow (by a mile).
 Charging Speed
 EcoFlow is the undisputed champion here. The Delta Pro charges at up to 3,000W via 240V AC (0-100% in 1.8 hours), takes up to 1,600W solar, and can combine AC + solar for up to 6,500W total input. That's a full charge in about 35 minutes if you max everything out.
 Jackery is solid: 1,800W AC charging (2 hours to full) and 1,400W solar input. Not the fastest, but more than adequate.
 Bluetti is slow: 400W AC charging stock (5-6 hours), or 800W with a second charger. Solar input is capped at 700W. If you camp in cloudy conditions or need quick turnaround between uses, this is a real limitation.

 [What Should You Remember?](#what-should-you-remember)
 RV season in Ontario runs from the May long weekend to Thanksgiving, and the electrical pedestals at most provincial parks top out at 30 amps. That is enough for lights, a fridge and a laptop charger. Add a roof air conditioner or an induction cooktop and the pedestal breaker trips. A portable power station fills that gap, and unlike a gas generator it can run inside the coach or under the awning with no exhaust at all. If you already own a small unit for tailgates, our [portable power station guide](/articles/best-portable-power-station-2026/) explains where those compact models stop being useful. This comparison covers five units that hold up under real trailer loads.
 The picks below were sorted on four measured numbers: continuous AC output, surge output, usable capacity and charge time. Real campsite loads matter far more than the number on the box. A 13,500 BTU roof air conditioner draws about 1,500W running and spikes past 3,000W on compressor startup, so a station rated at 1,000W will not get it off the line no matter what the marketing claims. Runtime figures here are calculated at 85 percent inverter efficiency, which is where most lithium units land under a steady 500W load. There is a second use case worth naming. [Outage statistics](/articles/emergency-power-statistics-2026/) show that the same battery you carry in the trailer can keep a furnace fan and fridge alive at home during a winter storm.
 Safety rules do not soften because the power source is smaller. RV shore inlets, transfer switches and any permanent wiring in a trailer fall under Ontario electrical rules, and the [Electrical Safety Authority](https://esasafe.com/) requires a licensed electrician for anything beyond plugging into an existing outlet. Carbon monoxide is the other hard line. Battery stations produce none, which is why one can sit on the dinette table, but a gas generator stays outside and away from windows and vents. The [CSA Group](https://www.csagroup.org/) publishes the standards behind both the appliances and the CO alarms you should have on board, and our [generator safety guide](/articles/generator-safety-tips/) covers placement distances in detail.
 Choosing comes down to three questions. How many watts does your largest single load need at startup? How many hours do you need it to run? How much weight can you lift into a storage bay? A 2,000Wh station weighs between 40 and 55 pounds, which one person can handle. Anything above 3,000Wh usually means two people or a dedicated cart. Solar input matters as well, since most Ontario parks enforce quiet hours and a 300W to 400W folding array will refill a mid-size unit in a full day of decent sun. Buy for the load you actually run, not the one you imagine running.
